A meta- analysis21 of low-molecular-weight heparins in major orthopaedic surgery found no evidence that giving the first dose pre- rather than postoperatively was more effective; there were similar risks for major bleeds. Either option is therefore acceptable; first dosage close to the time of sur- gery may be more effective but has been associated with increased risk of major bleeds. Low-molecular-weight heparins may also be more effective than unfractionated heparin in patients with major trauma.22 The optimum duration of prophylaxis is unclear.23 Proph- ylaxis is usually only continued during hospitalisation but extended prophylaxis may have a role, particularly in high-risk patients after orthopaedic surgery,8,10,11 or in very high-risk general surgical patients.8,11 After orthopaedic surgery there is an increased risk for DVT detected by venography up to a month after discharge, which may be reduced by low-molecular-weight heparin.24,25 However, the clinical significance of this finding has been questioned26 and a systematic review27 suggested that the benefit of extended prophylaxis may have been overesti- mated. A meta-analysis28 of 2 studies in patients having surgery for cancer also found a reduction in thrombosis when enoxaparin or dalteparin was given for 4 weeks. Oral anticoagulants have not been so widely used as sub- cutaneous heparin although US guidelines11 allow the use of adjusted-dose warfarin to give an international normal- ised ratio (INR) of 2.0 to 3.0 in patients having hip or knee replacement surgery. Antiplatelet drugs such as aspirin have been considered less effective antithrombotics than anticoagulants in the venous circulation and to be of limited value in preventing venous thromboembolism. An overview29 of randomised trials of antiplatelet therapy (mainly aspirin) available up to March 1990 and a more recent placebo-controlled trial30 of aspirin in patients having hip surgery have suggested that antiplatelet drugs reduce the risk of venous throm- boembolism and should thus be considered in high-risk patients. However, both reports have been criticised and, while some guidelines recommend the use of aspirin,8 oth- ers suggest it should not be used alone since other methods are generally more effective.11 Long-term use of low-dose aspirin appears to have little effect on the incidence of ve- nous thromboembolism.31 Direct thrombin inhibitors have been tried.32 Desirudin has been shown to be effective and was reported to be superior to both low-dose subcutaneous heparin and to a low-molecular-weight heparin in patients undergoing hip replacement surgery.
